cisco.name: Cisco
cisco.tagline: IOS / IOS-XE — Catalyst switching and ISR routing
cisco.gear: Catalyst switches · ISR / IOS-XE routers · ASA / Firepower
cisco.description: Build a network the Cisco way: an IOS-XE router at the edge, a Catalyst L3 switch for the LAN, VLANs and SVIs for segmentation, OSPF internally, PAT to the internet, ACLs and Layer-2 hardening for security, STP + EtherChannel + HSRP for redundancy, and IKEv2 IPsec for site-to-site. Every step includes the exact CLI, the show commands to prove it works, and the pitfalls that cause real-world outages.

fortinet.name: Fortinet
fortinet.description: Build a network the Fortinet way: a FortiGate NGFW as the all-in-one edge (routing, NAT, firewall, VPN, DHCP), FortiSwitch for the LAN via FortiLink, VLAN sub-interfaces for segmentation, OSPF internally, policy-based NAT and VIPs to the internet, firewall policies with UTM security profiles, FGCP for high availability, and route-based IPsec plus SSL-VPN for remote access. Every step includes the FortiOS config-tree CLI, the get/diagnose commands to prove it works, and the pitfalls that bite in the real world.

steps.title: Plan & IP Addressing
steps.what: A network build starts on paper, not on a console. Before you touch a device you decide the topology, the IP addressing scheme, the VLAN map, and a naming convention. A clean, room-to-grow address plan is the single biggest predictor of whether the rest of the build goes smoothly.
steps.why: Every later step — VLANs, routing, DHCP, NAT, firewall rules, VPN selectors — references these subnets. Get the plan right once and everything downstream is mechanical. Get it wrong (overlapping subnets, no growth room, a flat network) and you re-address later under pressure, usually during an outage.

cisco.gear: Design artifact — produce this before you console into anything.
cli: ! Example plan — single site, ~25 users, RFC1918 space
verify: Confirm no subnet overlaps and every VLAN has room to double
Reserve a management VLAN (99) that is NOT the default VLAN 1
Pick router-ids up front (loopbacks) so OSPF is deterministic
pitfalls: Using VLAN 1 for real traffic — leave it unused, it is a security default target
Sizing every VLAN /24 out of habit when guest/IoT could be smaller and data larger
No documented naming standard, so device configs drift and nobody can read them later
cisco.study: Stay fluent converting prefix to mask to wildcard, keep everything inside the RFC1918 ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16), and leave VLAN 1 and the native VLAN unused — they are common attack defaults.

fortinet.gear: Design artifact — produce this before you log into the FortiGate.
cli: # Example plan — single site, ~25 users, RFC1918 space
# Convention: gateway .1, FortiGate ports named by role
verify: Confirm no subnet overlaps and every VLAN has room to double
Plan a dedicated mgmt VLAN reachable only from trusted hosts
Decide policy-NAT vs central-NAT mode before building policies
pitfalls: Assuming the FortiGate routes freely between segments — traffic is denied until a firewall policy allows it
Not planning which physical port becomes the FortiLink to the FortiSwitch
Sizing guest identically to data when guest should be isolated and small
fortinet.study: Work inside the RFC1918 ranges and keep the FortiGate model in mind: routing and firewall policy are separate decisions — a route makes traffic possible, a policy makes it permitted.

steps.title: Device Access & Management
steps.what: Before the device forwards a single packet, secure how you administer it: a hostname, strong local credentials, encrypted remote access (SSH/HTTPS), a management interface, and a login banner. This is day-zero hardening.
steps.why: An edge device reachable over Telnet with a default password is compromised within minutes of going online. Locking down management first means every subsequent change is made over an encrypted, authenticated channel — and it is the first thing an auditor checks.

cisco.gear: Catalyst switch / IOS-XE router — console cable for first access.
pitfalls: Forgetting the RSA key — SSH silently refuses to start without hostname + domain-name + key
Leaving 'transport input telnet' or 'all' on the vty lines
Configuring everything, then losing it all to a reload because you never ran 'write memory'
cisco.study: SSH needs three things before it will start: a hostname, a domain-name, and an RSA key of at least 768 bits. 'enable secret' protects privileged EXEC, and privilege 15 grants full access.

fortinet.gear: FortiGate — console or the default 192.168.1.99 mgmt IP for first access.
pitfalls: Leaving the default admin account with no password
Setting 'allowaccess' with http/telnet, or enabling admin access on the WAN interface
No trusthost, so the admin account is reachable from any source IP
fortinet.study: Core FortiOS habits: the config tree (config, edit, set, next, end), 'trusthost' to restrict admin sources, 'admin-sport' to move the GUI off 443, and never enabling administrative access on an untrusted interface.

steps.title: Interfaces & VLANs
steps.what: Bring up Layer 2: create your VLANs, assign access ports to them, and build an 802.1Q trunk to carry all VLANs to the router/firewall. This turns one physical switch into several isolated broadcast domains.
steps.why: VLANs are the foundation of segmentation and the single most impactful control you can apply. Without them the network is flat — one infected guest laptop can reach every server. The trunk is what lets a single cable carry all those segments up to the routing layer.

pitfalls: Forgetting to add a VLAN to 'switchport trunk allowed vlan' — traffic for it is silently dropped on the trunk
Native VLAN mismatch between the two ends of a trunk
Enabling PortFast on a trunk or uplink port (invites loops)
cisco.study: Access vs trunk, 802.1Q tagging, and the native (untagged) VLAN are the fundamentals. Hardcode 'switchport mode' so DTP can't auto-negotiate a trunk you didn't intend.

fortinet.gear: FortiGate VLAN sub-interfaces (over a hardware switch or FortiLink to FortiSwitch).
pitfalls: Choosing a parent 'interface' that is not a switch/hardware-switch member
VLAN ID on the FortiGate sub-interface not matching the tag on the FortiSwitch port
Overlapping the sub-interface subnet with an existing interface
fortinet.study: On FortiGate a VLAN is a sub-interface bound to a physical/aggregate parent with its own vlanid; the sub-interface IP becomes that VLAN's gateway. FortiSwitch VLANs are pushed over FortiLink from the FortiGate.

steps.title: Inter-VLAN Routing & DHCP
steps.what: Give each VLAN a default gateway and hand out addresses. On Cisco that means enabling routing and creating an SVI per VLAN plus DHCP pools; on Fortinet the VLAN interfaces are already routable and you attach a DHCP server to each.
steps.why: VLANs isolate traffic, but users still need to reach servers, printers, and the internet — that requires a router interface in each VLAN. DHCP then removes the manual, error-prone job of statically addressing every endpoint.

cisco.gear: Catalyst L3 switch (SVIs) or router-on-a-stick sub-interfaces.
pitfalls: Forgetting 'ip routing' — SVIs come up but the switch won't route between them
Not excluding the gateway/infra range, so DHCP leases out 10.10.10.1 to a client
Assuming inter-VLAN reachability is fine security — you still want ACLs (next steps)
cisco.study: Two ways to route between VLANs: SVIs on an L3 switch (this example) or router-on-a-stick (sub-interfaces with 'encapsulation dot1q'). Always protect static ranges with 'ip dhcp excluded-address'.

fortinet.gear: FortiGate — routes between its own interfaces; DHCP server per VLAN.
pitfalls: Expecting VLANs to talk to each other automatically — you still need a firewall policy between them
Binding the DHCP server to the wrong sub-interface
DNS-service set to 'default' when the FortiGate isn't allowed out to resolve
fortinet.study: The FortiGate routes between its own interfaces, but every inter-VLAN flow still needs a firewall policy. DHCP is configured per interface under 'config system dhcp server'.

steps.title: Routing (Static + OSPF)
steps.what: Point a default route at the ISP so the network can reach the internet, and run OSPF internally so multiple L3 devices learn each other's subnets automatically instead of by hand.
steps.why: A default route is what turns a LAN into an internet-connected network. Dynamic routing (OSPF) keeps the routing table correct as you add subnets or links, and reconverges automatically when something fails — no manual route edits during an outage.

pitfalls: Using a subnet mask instead of a wildcard mask in the OSPF 'network' statement
Mismatched area numbers between neighbors — no adjacency forms
Forgetting 'default-information originate', so internal routers never learn the default route
cisco.study: OSPF essentials: wildcard masks in network statements, every area touching area 0, router-id order (manual, then highest loopback, then highest interface), 'passive-interface' on user VLANs, and administrative distance 110.

pitfalls: Static default route missing the outbound 'device', so it never installs
OSPF 'redistribute static' needed if you want the default advertised to neighbors
Two equal static routes creating unintended ECMP — set 'priority'/'distance' to steer
fortinet.study: FortiOS static routes carry a distance and a priority (both affect selection); OSPF lives under one 'config router ospf' tree with area and network sub-tables. Redistribution is explicit.

steps.title: NAT / PAT
steps.what: Translate your private RFC1918 addresses to the single public IP from your ISP so many hosts share one address (PAT), and optionally publish an internal service to the internet with a static/destination NAT (port forward).
steps.why: You get one public IP and have dozens of devices; NAT is what makes that work. Port forwarding lets you host a service (VPN endpoint, web app) while keeping everything else hidden. Every forwarded port is attack surface, so you forward only what's needed.

cli: ip nat inside source list 1 interface gi0/1 overload
! static port-forward: public :443 -> internal web server
ip nat inside source static tcp 10.10.10.20 443 interface gi0/1 443
pitfalls: Forgetting to mark interfaces 'ip nat inside' / 'ip nat outside' — nothing translates
A NAT ACL that is too broad and overlaps VPN traffic (needs NAT exemption later)
Confusing the inside-local vs inside-global address in troubleshooting
cisco.study: 'overload' = PAT (port address translation). Keep the four NAT address types straight (inside/outside by local/global), know dynamic PAT vs static NAT, and mind NAT's order of operations relative to routing and crypto.

fortinet.gear: FortiGate — NAT lives in the firewall policy and in VIPs.
cli: # Source NAT (outbound) is a flag on the firewall policy
# Destination NAT / port-forward via a VIP
pitfalls: Forgetting 'set nat enable' on the outbound policy — traffic is allowed but not translated
Creating a VIP but no policy that uses the VIP as the destination address
Mixing policy-NAT and central-NAT mode expectations
fortinet.study: FortiGate does policy-based NAT by default: SNAT is 'set nat enable' (optionally with IP pools), DNAT is a VIP referenced as the dstaddr of a firewall policy. Central NAT is the alternative model.

steps.title: Firewall Policy & Hardening
steps.what: Enforce who can talk to whom. Restrict inter-VLAN traffic (e.g. guest can reach the internet but not internal subnets), apply threat inspection on internet-bound traffic, and harden Layer 2 against common attacks.
steps.why: Segmentation only helps if a policy enforces it. This is where you contain a compromised device to its own VLAN, block lateral movement, and inspect outbound traffic for malware. Layer-2 hardening (port-security, DHCP snooping) stops the attacks that bypass Layer-3 rules entirely.

cisco.gear: Catalyst switch (ACLs + L2 hardening); ASA/Firepower for full NGFW.
pitfalls: ACL rule order — the implicit 'deny any' at the bottom drops what you forgot to permit
Applying an ACL in the wrong direction (in vs out) relative to the interface
Enabling DHCP snooping without trusting the uplink port toward the real DHCP server
cisco.study: Extended ACLs match source+dest+protocol+port and always end in an implicit 'deny any'. Pair them with L2 controls: port-security, DHCP snooping, and Dynamic ARP Inspection.

fortinet.gear: FortiGate — firewall policies with UTM security profiles.
pitfalls: Policy order — FortiGate matches top-down and stops at the first match; a broad allow above a deny wins
Enabling 'utm-status' but forgetting to attach the AV/IPS profiles
Relying on the implicit deny without an explicit deny/log policy for visibility
fortinet.study: FortiGate evaluates policies top-down, first match wins, with an implicit deny at the end. Security profiles (AntiVirus, IPS, Web Filter, Application Control) attach to a policy, and 'diagnose debug flow' shows a packet's fate.

steps.title: High Availability & Redundancy
steps.what: Remove single points of failure at Layers 2 and 3: a loop-free redundant switch topology (STP), bundled uplinks (EtherChannel/LAG), and gateway redundancy so a device failure doesn't take the default gateway offline.
steps.why: One switch, one uplink, one gateway means one failure equals a full outage. Redundancy plus fast reconvergence keeps the network up through a failed link or a rebooted device — the difference between a non-event and a company-wide outage.

pitfalls: EtherChannel mode mismatch (active/passive/on) — the bundle stays down or, worse, loops
HSRP virtual IP not matching the address you handed clients as their gateway
Never setting a root bridge, so STP elects one by lowest MAC (often the oldest switch)
cisco.study: Know RSTP port roles/states and root-bridge election, LACP (active/passive) vs PAgP vs static 'on' for EtherChannel, and first-hop redundancy protocols — HSRP (active/standby, preempt), VRRP, and GLBP.

fortinet.gear: Two FortiGates in FGCP HA + aggregate link to the switch.
pitfalls: Heartbeat interfaces not directly connected between the two units, or mismatched hbdev config
Mismatched firmware/hardware between the HA members — the cluster won't form
Leaving 'override enable' with equal priorities, causing failback flapping
fortinet.study: FGCP HA: active-passive vs active-active, dedicated heartbeat interfaces, 'session-pickup' for stateful failover, and 'override' controlling whether the higher-priority unit reclaims primary. LACP aggregate interfaces bundle links to the switch.

steps.title: VPN (Site-to-Site + Remote Access)
steps.what: Build encrypted tunnels: an IPsec site-to-site tunnel to connect another office, and remote-access VPN so employees reach internal resources securely from anywhere.
steps.why: VPNs extend the trusted network over the untrusted internet without exposing services directly. Site-to-site stitches offices into one routable network; remote-access replaces risky port-forwards (never expose RDP directly) with an authenticated, encrypted entry point.

cisco.gear: IOS-XE router (IKEv2 IPsec); AnyConnect for remote access.
cli: crypto ipsec transform-set TS esp-aes 256 esp-sha256-hmac
pitfalls: Interesting-traffic ACL must be an exact mirror on both peers, or Phase 2 never comes up
Mismatched proposals, DH group, or PSK between the two ends
No NAT exemption for VPN traffic, so packets get PATed instead of encrypted
cisco.study: IPsec has two phases: IKE (Phase 1) builds the secure channel, IPsec (Phase 2) protects the data. Mind transform sets and the crypto ACL as 'interesting traffic'; IKEv2 is preferred over IKEv1.

pitfalls: Route-based IPsec needs BOTH a static route to the remote subnet and firewall policies in each direction
Phase 1/Phase 2 proposal or DH-group mismatch with the peer
Phase 2 selectors (src/dst subnet) not matching the far end
fortinet.study: FortiGate prefers route-based (interface-mode) IPsec: the tunnel becomes a virtual interface you route and policy over. SSL-VPN (web or tunnel mode) is the usual remote-access method.

steps.title: Verify, Monitor & Troubleshoot
steps.what: Prove the build works end to end, then set up the telemetry to keep it healthy: connectivity and path tests, centralized logging (syslog), time sync (NTP), and SNMP for a monitoring platform. Finally, learn the go-to troubleshooting commands.
steps.why: A config that looks right isn't proven until it's tested. Baselining now tells you what 'normal' looks like, logging and NTP give you an accurate audit trail, and SNMP feeds a dashboard so you learn about problems before users do. The troubleshooting commands are what you reach for at 2 a.m.

pitfalls: No NTP, so log timestamps across devices don't line up and correlation is impossible
SNMP community left as 'public' / RW — a trivial reconnaissance and attack vector
Ignoring err-disabled ports (show interfaces status err-disabled) after port-security trips
cisco.study: 'show ip interface brief' is your first-look command; ping/traceroute for reachability; syslog severity levels 0-7; SNMP v2c vs v3 (v3 adds auth+encryption); and CDP/LLDP for neighbor discovery.

pitfalls: Assuming disk logging is on — many FortiGate models log to memory only until you point them at disk/FortiAnalyzer
Leaving 'diagnose debug flow' or 'diagnose sniffer' running after troubleshooting (CPU + noise)
SNMP community reachable from any host instead of a locked-down collector
fortinet.study: Three FortiOS command families: 'get' (state), 'show' (config), 'diagnose' (deep troubleshooting). 'diagnose debug flow' traces a packet through the policy engine; FortiView and FortiAnalyzer add the long-term visibility SNMP alone can't.
